title: maxExchangeRate is a share-to-asset rate pair denominated in the underlying's own decimals, making the encoding a 12-order-of-magnitude hazard
content:
Comparing the `setMaxExchangeRate` calls across instances reveals the parameter's actual shape. The two RLUSD vaults use `(1e18, 3e18)` for a 3-RLUSD ceiling (A...7.6.4.1, A...7.7.4.1). The AUSD vault uses `(1e18, 2e6)` for 2 AUSD (A...7.4.4.1), and the PYUSD vaults use `(1e18, 3e6)` and `(1e18, 4e6)` for 3 and 4 PYUSD (A...7.5.4.1, A...3.1.7.3.2.4.3).

The two arguments are a **ratio**: shares in 18 decimals, assets in the underlying token's native decimals. RLUSD is an 18-decimal token, so 3 RLUSD is `3e18`; USDC, PYUSD and AUSD are 6-decimal, so the same nominal ceiling is `3e6`.

That makes the encoding fragile in an asymmetric and dangerous way. Writing `3e6` where `3e18` was meant sets a ceiling a trillion times too low, and deposits revert immediately — annoying but loud and safe. Writing `3e18` where `3e6` was meant sets a ceiling a trillion times too high, which silently disables the protection entirely while every deposit succeeds. The failure directions are not equally visible, and the dangerous one is the one that produces no symptom.

The Artifact's mitigation is to state the intent in prose next to every call — "ensures 1 share can represent at most 3 RLUSD" — so a reviewer can check the literal against a human-readable claim without knowing the token's decimals. That convention is the only defence documented, and it is why the prose sentence beside each call is load-bearing rather than decorative.

A safer interface would take the ceiling in a fixed unit and read decimals from the token, removing the class of error entirely.
description: RLUSD vaults pass (1e18, 3e18) while USDC, PYUSD and AUSD vaults pass (1e18, Xe6) — the same 3x ceiling is written differently depending on the asset's decimals.
